strengths: Originality: Connecting relative-likelihood parameter posteriors, supremum projection, and a learnable Dirichlet possibility function is an interesting synthesis. Equations (6)–(10) provide a concrete conceptual starting point for second-order prediction.

Soundness of the tractable calculation: Under the implemented parameter restriction αk > 1, the closed-form inner maximizer is correctly derived. Figure 1 makes the resulting training update straightforward to implement.

Significance: The empirical results suggest a useful classification loss. DAPPr improves CIFAR-10-LT accuracy at ρ = 0.01 from F-EDL’s 63.73% to 68.81%, and achieves competitive uncertainty rankings across several datasets. Five-seed results and regularization ablations are valuable.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript has a coherent progression from possibility theory to implementation, with explicit equations, pseudocode, dataset splits, and selected hyperparameters. The public benchmark experiments raise no apparent material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—posterior approximation is not established: Equation (11) reduces the projected posterior at a training input to its single-label likelihood, discarding dependence on the remaining dataset. The manuscript does not establish that learning this surrogate at training inputs approximates Equation (7) at unseen inputs. Indeed, if the same independent-fitting premise holds at an unseen input, its prediction can vary without changing training loss, yielding a completely uninformative projected posterior. This leaves the central claim of principled test-time epistemic uncertainty unsupported.

Soundness—one-sided divergence does not identify the desired uncertainty: Dmax(gψ || g*) vanishes for any normalized gψ bounded above by g*, including excessively concentrated possibilities. Thus minimizing it does not ensure faithful posterior uncertainty. The claim that uninformative initialization resolves this is not demonstrated, and the implemented α = softplus(logits) + 1 cannot represent the paper’s ignorance function, which requires α = 0. Shared neural parameters also prevent treating optimization as independent pointwise reductions.

Soundness—regularizer does not prevent the stated pathology: Section 4.4 motivates Equation (16) as preventing unbounded precision, but it penalizes only incorrect-class parameters. For a separable example, the correct-class parameter can grow without bound while this penalty stays fixed and the surrogate divergence approaches zero. Consequently, the claimed control of total evidence is not supplied by this regularizer. The final epistemic score K/α0 is also introduced without a derivation connecting it to the projected posterior or a validated uncertainty property.

Evidence for the approximation is insufficient: Appendix C uses three-epoch fine-tuning with a soft-label example included in each batch, without demonstrating satisfaction of Φθ(x) = p or attainment of the constrained infimum. Random perturbations do not establish uniform accuracy over the simplex. Moreover, comparing a loss difference of 0.25 with a total loss of 320 is not the relevant criterion: posterior ratios depend exponentially on absolute loss differences, while the common loss offset cancels.

Evaluation supports ranking performance more strongly than epistemic validity: Confidence AUPR treats correct predictions as positives and therefore benefits from improved accuracy. No calibration or controlled aleatoric-versus-epistemic evaluation establishes the claimed uncertainty interpretation. Figure 3’s data-size trend on one dataset cannot confirm the theoretical foundation. Results are also mixed: F-EDL outperforms DAPPr on both CIFAR-100 OOD tasks. Timing and memory measurements are absent despite efficiency being a central motivation.

Reproducibility, positioning, and limitations need improvement: The code-availability sentence contains no link; optimizer, learning-rate schedule, augmentation, and precise hyperparameter-selection criteria are insufficiently specified. Several comparisons import published results without fully establishing matched protocols. Blanket claims that competing second-order methods lack principled foundations need more careful qualification. Although conflicting duplicate labels are acknowledged, the more consequential limitations of posterior identifiability and unseen-input approximation are not addressed. These unresolved central issues outweigh the promising empirical gains.

strengths: Originality: Connecting a projected possibilistic parameter posterior to a learned Dirichlet possibility function is an interesting conceptual contribution. The closed-form inner maximizer in Proposition 1 is correct under the implemented restriction αk > 1.

Significance: The method is a simple replacement loss requiring a single predictive network. Reported improvements are substantial in some settings: CIFAR-10-LT accuracy at ρ = 0.01 increases from F-EDL’s 63.73% to 68.81%, and CUB accuracy improves from R-EDL’s 51.83% to 55.95%. These results suggest practical value even independently of the theoretical interpretation.

Evaluation: Experiments span standard classification, class imbalance, corruptions, and fine-grained datasets, with means and standard deviations over five seeds. The regularization ablations and combination with ensembles provide useful additional evidence.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript has a clear conceptual progression, compact implementation pseudocode, an explicit proof of Proposition 1, and dataset splits and regularization coefficients in Appendix B. No concrete research-ethics violation is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—posterior approximation does not identify epistemic uncertainty: Equation (8) has zero divergence whenever gψ ≤ g*, including overly concentrated functions that exclude plausible predictions. Thus minimizing this objective need not recover the posterior’s uncertainty. The claim that uninformative initialization resolves this is unsupported, and the implemented α = softplus(logits) + 1 cannot represent the stated ignorance function, which requires α = 0. Under the same independent-fitting assumption extended to an unseen input, its projected posterior is identically one, making every normalized learned possibility function a zero-loss solution. The central connection between the practical predictor and reliable out-of-sample epistemic uncertainty therefore remains unestablished.

Soundness—the regularizer does not prevent the claimed unbounded precision: Section 4.4 motivates Equation (16) as preventing arbitrarily large total evidence, but it penalizes only incorrect-class evidence. For a sample with true class t, the implemented detached-maximizer gradient with respect to αt is log[α0(αt−1)/(αt(α0−1))], which is strictly negative when other-class evidence is positive. The regularizer contributes no opposing gradient in this coordinate. Consequently, the per-sample update continues to increase true-class evidence without a finite stationary point, directly undermining the stated justification for this regularizer and the interpretation of K/α0.

Soundness—validation of the key approximation is insufficient: Appendix C uses three epochs of fine-tuning with a sample inserted into every batch, but does not establish that Φθ(x) actually equals the prescribed p or that the constrained infimum in Equation (11) is reached. The perturbation distribution and count are unspecified. Moreover, comparing a loss deviation of 0.25 with an aggregate loss of 320 is not the relevant criterion: the approximation concerns absolute differences in log possibility, and a difference of 0.25 changes the corresponding likelihood factor by about 22%. Figure 5 does not validate the approximation uniformly over the simplex.

Significance and evidential scope: Ranking accuracy and OOD AUPR do not establish the claimed separation of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Figure 3 provides one data-size experiment against an unstable EDL baseline, without uncertainty bars or a controlled irreducible-noise setting; it cannot confirm the broad theoretical claims. Gains are also not universal: on CIFAR-100, DAPPr trails F-EDL on both OOD datasets. Much of the standard-dataset comparison imports baseline numbers from prior publications, without enough protocol detail to establish matched training and tuning. Confidence AUPR treats correct predictions as positives and is affected by classification accuracy, so higher values alone do not isolate better uncertainty estimation.

Reproducibility: Appendix B omits important details including the optimizer, learning-rate schedule, augmentation, checkpoint-selection criterion, and full baseline search spaces and selection rules. Appendix C is particularly difficult to reproduce. The abstract’s code-release statement has no URL. The pseudocode helps reproduce the loss, but not the reported comparisons; computational-efficiency claims also lack measured runtime or memory evidence.

Presentation, positioning, and limitations: The manuscript repeatedly characterizes competing second-order methods as lacking principled foundations without sufficiently distinguishing their actual assumptions and guarantees. It acknowledges the conflicting-label caveat, which is useful, but does not adequately discuss the more consequential non-identifiability and extrapolation limitations. Calling the numerical smallness of λ evidence of minimal tuning is also unjustified because its scale depends on the loss. Overall, the practical merits warrant further investigation, but the unsupported central theoretical claims and incomplete experimental controls prevent acceptance.

strengths: Originality: Projecting a relative-likelihood possibility function from parameter space to prediction space, then learning a Dirichlet approximation, is an interesting conceptual connection. Equations (6)–(10) provide a useful starting point for studying alternatives to Bayesian predictive uncertainty.

Significance: The reported empirical gains are meaningful in several settings. DAPPr improves CIFAR-10-LT accuracy at imbalance ratio 0.01 from F-EDL’s 63.73% to 68.81%, and improves CUB accuracy from R-EDL’s 51.83% to 55.95%. Evaluation spans standard, imbalanced, corrupted, and fine-grained image datasets, with five-seed reporting.

Presentation and implementation: The manuscript explains the possibilistic construction accessibly. The closed-form inner maximizer is straightforward under the implemented parameter constraints, and Figure 1 provides concise pseudocode, including the essential stop-gradient operation. The method requires only one predictive network.

Experimental transparency: The paper identifies borrowed versus reproduced baseline results, supplies dataset splits and regularization coefficients, and includes regularizer and data-size ablations. The use of established image benchmarks raises no apparent material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—posterior matching does not identify uncertainty: Equation (8) minimizes Dmax(gψ || g*), which vanishes whenever gψ ≤ g*. This permits arbitrarily narrower approximations and therefore does not establish faithful posterior uncertainty. For example, if g* is a Dirichlet possibility function with parameters α, then parameters tα produce g*^t ≤ g* for any t ≥ 1, while K/(tα0) tends to zero. The assertion that uninformative initialization prevents this behavior is not proved for shared neural-network parameters; moreover, α = softplus(logits) + 1 cannot represent the stated ignorance function α = 0.

Soundness—the tractable approximation loses the central epistemic connection: Under Equation (11), the training-point posterior becomes proportional to p_y, independent of support from other observations. Under the analogous independent-fitting assumption at an unseen input, the projected posterior would instead be completely uninformative. The paper does not explain or establish why a network trained only on the former targets approximates the latter posterior at test inputs. Thus the implemented loss is motivated by a posterior construction, but its claimed principled test-time epistemic interpretation remains unsupported.

Soundness—the regularizer does not prevent the claimed unbounded precision: Equation (16) penalizes only incorrect-class evidence. Holding those components fixed and increasing the true-class component leaves this penalty unchanged. The detached data-term gradient for the true-class component is log[α0(α_y − 1)/(α_y(α0 − 1))], which is negative for K > 1. Consequently, the implemented objective still pushes true-class evidence upward without a finite per-example optimum. This directly contradicts the stated rationale that the regularizer prevents arbitrarily large total evidence.

Evidence for the approximation is insufficient: Appendix C compares three-epoch fine-tuning outcomes rather than constrained global infima, does not report how accurately the imposed predictions are achieved, and leaves the number and distribution of soft-label perturbations unspecified. Comparing a loss difference of approximately 0.25 to a total loss near 320 is also not the relevant justification: absolute loss differences enter the exponential posterior, and 0.25 corresponds to a multiplicative factor of about 0.78. The experiment does not bound the approximation error needed by the derivation.

Evaluation establishes useful rankings more convincingly than reliable uncertainty: Confidence AUPR is influenced by the fraction of correct predictions, so accuracy gains alone can improve it. Calibration or selective-risk evaluations would help separate these effects. Figure 3’s decreasing uncertainty on one dataset does not establish epistemic validity or resolve the theoretical concerns above. OOD superiority is also mixed: F-EDL exceeds DAPPr on both CIFAR-100 OOD datasets in Table 2, and several gains elsewhere are within reported variability.

Reproducibility and comparison gaps remain: The abstract’s promised code link is blank. Optimizer and learning-rate schedule details, augmentation, baseline search ranges, and the precise validation criterion for selecting hyperparameters are not adequately specified. Several main comparisons import results from prior papers without establishing complete protocol equivalence. Computational-efficiency claims are plausible from the architecture but lack measured runtime or memory comparisons.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript repeatedly describes competing second-order methods as lacking principled foundations without sufficiently distinguishing their existing derivations from the particular guarantees being sought here. It acknowledges conflicting duplicate inputs, but does not adequately discuss the more consequential approximation, identifiability, and unbounded-evidence limitations. The promising empirical contribution does not currently support the stronger central claim of resolving the rigor–efficiency dilemma.

strengths: Originality: Projecting a possibilistic parameter posterior into prediction space and deriving a tractable Dirichlet training rule is an interesting synthesis. The closed-form maximizer in Proposition 1 is justified under the implemented parameter constraints, and the stop-gradient implementation follows the stated Danskin argument.

Significance: The method is simple and potentially useful. Reported improvements include CIFAR-10-LT accuracy of 68.81% versus 63.73% for F-EDL and CUB accuracy of 55.95% versus 51.83% for R-EDL. Evaluation spans classification, OOD detection, corruption shifts, and language-model question answering, generally with five-seed results.

Presentation and practical reproducibility: The manuscript provides accessible preliminaries, concise pseudocode, regularizer ablations, dataset splits, and regularization schedules. Table 12 supports the practical efficiency claim: DAPPr has essentially the same training and inference costs as cross-entropy.
weaknesses: Soundness—the objective does not identify the claimed uncertainty target. Equation (8) has zero divergence whenever the learned possibility function lies below the reference, including functions much sharper than that reference. For example, a normalized reference raised to any power greater than one has zero divergence against the reference. Consequently, minimizing this objective need not recover its epistemic uncertainty. The uninformative-initialization argument does not resolve this ambiguity, particularly because the implemented family excludes that initialization.

Soundness—the regularizer does not prevent the overconcentration it is introduced to address. Equation (16) penalizes only incorrect-class parameters. Holding these fixed while increasing the true-class parameter without bound leaves the regularizer unchanged, permits arbitrarily sharp predictions, and sends the reported epistemic uncertainty K/alpha_0 to zero. Moreover, with alpha_k > 1, decreasing concentration cannot approach the total-ignorance function defined in Section 3: the limiting all-ones parameter vector still gives a nonuniform possibility function. These issues undermine the central interpretation of the learned concentration.

Soundness—the approximation removes the dataset dependence that motivates the framework. Under Equation (11), the training-point target becomes proportional to p_y, independent of the other observations. No result connects fitting these local targets to the projected posterior at unseen inputs. Under an analogous interpolation assumption at a new input, equally good training fits can yield arbitrary predictions there, making the exact projected posterior uninformative. The paper needs to explain how its learned predictor approximates that target rather than merely extrapolating a supervised loss.

The validation of Equation (11) in Appendix D is insufficient. Three epochs of fine-tuning with randomly sampled soft labels neither establish constrained infima nor verify that the prediction constraint is actually satisfied. The number and distribution of perturbations and constraint residuals are unreported. Comparing loss changes with the total training loss is also insufficient: additive changes in log possibility affect likelihood ratios through exponentiation, regardless of their small percentage of the total loss.

Empirical evidence supports useful discrimination more strongly than principled uncertainty decomposition. Correct-prediction AUPR is influenced by classification accuracy and does not establish calibration or separation of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Figure 5 provides one data-size experiment without uncertainty bars or controlled aleatoric noise. Several baselines perform strikingly poorly, including DUQ at 1.55% CUB accuracy, and the regularizer-transfer ablation collapses EDL almost to chance; these outcomes require implementation and loss-scale diagnostics before supporting broad superiority or claims that the regularizer is theoretically unique.

Reproducibility and limitations remain incomplete. The abstract's code-availability statement has no link. Baseline search ranges and selection criteria are mostly unspecified, and important training details are omitted or delegated to prior work. The acknowledged conflicting-label limitation is useful, but the manuscript does not adequately discuss objective non-identifiability or uncertainty generalization; dismissing low-capacity uncertainty estimation as secondary is unjustified. The generic impact statement raises no evident material ethical concern, but the strong reliability claims exceed the demonstrated guarantees. Overall, the promising practical results do not compensate for these unresolved weaknesses in the central theoretical claim.

strengths: Originality: The combination of a possibilistic parameter posterior, supremum projection into prediction space, and amortized Dirichlet approximation offers an interesting perspective on second-order uncertainty prediction. The reference target in Eqs. (6)–(7) is explicitly defined.

Technical merits and presentation: Proposition 1 gives a straightforward closed-form inner maximizer under the implemented parameter constraints. The pseudocode clearly includes the stop-gradient operation needed for the Danskin-based update, making the practical method easy to understand.

Significance: The reported empirical gains are meaningful across several settings. DAPPr improves CIFAR-10-LT accuracy from 63.73% for F-EDL to 68.81%, and CUB accuracy from 51.83% for R-EDL to 55.95%. Experiments span classification, OOD detection, corruption shifts, and multiple-choice language-model evaluation, generally with five-seed reporting.

Practicality: Table 12 supports computational efficiency comparable to cross-entropy training. The regularizer ablations, dataset splits, and dataset-specific hyperparameters provide useful implementation evidence.
weaknesses: Soundness—matching the uncertainty target is not established. The paper explicitly notes that Dmax(gψ || g*) vanishes whenever gψ ≤ g*, including functions much sharper than the target. Consequently, minimizing Eq. (8) does not identify the target's epistemic uncertainty. The proposed justification through uninformative initialization is unavailable under the implemented αk > 1 parameterization, and shared-network optimization does not guarantee the claimed pointwise reduction only where the ordering is violated. This directly undermines the central claim of faithfully approximating a principled uncertainty target.

Soundness—the regularizer does not prevent the concentration pathology it is introduced to address. Under Eq. (12), a one-hot observation gives the normalized target g*(p) = p_y. Holding all wrong-class αk fixed above 1 and sending α_y to infinity leaves R unchanged while the surrogate max-divergence approaches zero. Thus arbitrarily concentrated predictions remain possible without additional regularization cost, although the target p_y remains broad. Moreover, αk > 1 excludes both this exact target's parameterization and total ignorance, which Eq. (1) represents using α = 0. The claim that K/α0 directly measures insufficient parameter knowledge therefore needs substantially more justification.

Soundness—the high-capacity approximation removes precisely the cross-sample coupling through which the dataset could constrain uncertainty. Eqs. (10)–(12) derive a surrogate only at labeled training inputs; there is no argument that its learned extension approximates Eq. (7) at unseen inputs. Under a sufficiently flexible model that can also change an unseen input's prediction without changing training loss, the projected target there is actually vacuous. Appendix D does not resolve this: three-epoch fine-tuning with a repeated soft-label example does not establish the hard constraint Φθ(x) = p or the constrained infimum. Comparing loss deviations with the total loss also does not bound the relevant log-possibility error.

Evaluation and significance: The extensive ranking results support a useful empirical loss, but do not validate the claimed epistemic/aleatoric interpretation. Figure 5 examines one dataset against an unstable EDL baseline without uncertainty bars; monotonicity of an aggregate score alone does not establish correct uncertainty decomposition. Confidence AUPR also depends on classification accuracy because correct predictions are the positive class. Controlled experiments with known uncertainty, direct projected-target comparisons on tractable models, and comparisons at matched accuracy would better isolate the claimed contribution. Superiority is not universal: F-EDL exceeds DAPPr on both CIFAR-100 OOD benchmarks in Table 1.

Reproducibility and comparison quality: The abstract's code-availability statement contains no link. Although many settings are supplied, optimizer and augmentation details, exact baseline search spaces and selection criteria, and the sampling and constraint-fit details for Appendix D remain insufficiently specified. Some baseline failures are severe, such as DUQ's 1.55% CUB accuracy and EDL with the proposed regularizer's 0.78%; these require diagnosis before being interpreted as evidence of framework-specific superiority.

Presentation, limitations, and ethics: The manuscript is generally readable but repeatedly presents empirical observations as confirming theoretical rigor. Claims that alternative second-order methods lack principled foundations are overly sweeping, and declaring uncertainty quantification secondary in low-capacity settings dismisses a relevant limitation. The acknowledged conflicting-label case is useful, but limitations of target identification, test-input extrapolation, and the uncertainty scores remain insufficiently discussed. I identify no material ethical violation in the described experiments; the decisive concerns are technical and evidential.

strengths: Originality: Defining a relative-likelihood possibility function over parameters and projecting it into prediction space provides an interesting perspective on second-order prediction. The resulting Dirichlet training rule is a potentially useful methodological contribution.

Soundness of the local derivation: Under the stated approximation and implemented constraint αk > 1, Proposition 1 gives the correct inner maximizer. The detached maximizer in Figure 1 implements the intended Danskin gradient efficiently.

Significance: The empirical improvements are meaningful in several settings. DAPPr improves CIFAR-10-LT accuracy from F-EDL’s 63.73% to 68.81% at ρ = 0.01, and exceeds the strongest listed single-model accuracy on both fine-grained datasets. Evaluation spans multiple architectures, dataset sizes, and an LLM benchmark, generally with five-seed results.

Presentation and practicality: The framework is organized clearly, with useful pseudocode, explicit uncertainty scores, regularizer ablations, and implementation details. Table 12 supports the practical efficiency claim: training and inference costs closely match cross-entropy.
weaknesses: Soundness—posterior matching is not established. Equation (8) has zero divergence whenever the learned possibility function lies below the target, including substantially sharper functions. It therefore does not identify the target’s uncertainty. The proposed uninformative initialization cannot be represented by the implemented αk > 1 family, and shared network updates need not preserve minimum commitment. Moreover, Equation (16) leaves correct-class evidence unpenalized: increasing that evidence without bound while holding wrong-class evidence fixed can drive the surrogate divergence toward zero and K/α0 toward zero. Thus the regularizer does not establish the claimed protection against arbitrary sharpness.

Soundness—the approximation removes the central dependence on parameter uncertainty. Equations (11)–(12) reduce the training-point target to exp(−ℓ(p,y)), which for one-hot cross-entropy is simply py, independently of the remaining dataset. No argument connects generalization of this label-based surrogate to the projected posterior at unseen inputs. Indeed, for a model class that can independently interpolate an unseen input while preserving training predictions, the uniform-prior projection there is total ignorance. The learned family cannot represent this. The paper needs a substantive account of the inductive assumptions that bridge this gap.

Validation of Equation (11) is insufficient. Appendix D compares three-epoch fine-tuning outcomes rather than constrained infima, does not report how accurately Φθ(x) = p is satisfied, and leaves the number and distribution of sampled soft labels unspecified. Small deviations relative to the total loss do not establish small posterior errors: an absolute log-loss deviation of 0.25 already changes an unnormalized possibility by a factor of approximately 0.78. This experiment does not validate uniform accuracy of the approximation.

The uncertainty interpretation remains partly heuristic. Section 5.3’s decreasing average uncertainty with increasing data is encouraging, but cannot establish epistemic validity or separation from aleatoric uncertainty. Similarly, the mode can still contain estimation error, so calling its uncertainty exclusively irreducible is unsupported. The assertion that decreasing α0 approaches total ignorance also conflicts with the implementation’s lower bound α0 > K; total ignorance in Equation (1) requires zero exponents.

Evaluation supports competitiveness more strongly than general superiority. F-EDL outperforms DAPPr on both CIFAR-100 OOD tasks, and several other differences overlap reported variability. Confidence AUPR treats correct predictions as positives and therefore changes with classification accuracy; improvements do not independently demonstrate improved uncertainty ranking. Extremely weak baselines, including 1.55% CUB accuracy for DUQ, also warrant diagnosis. Regularizer-swap failures alone do not prove that the regularizer is unique to possibility theory.

Reproducibility and limitations: The supplied manuscript ends its code-availability statement without a link. Appendix C omits several optimizer, preprocessing, and hyperparameter-selection details, including the validation criterion for selecting the reported best baseline configurations. The paper acknowledges conflicting duplicate labels and capacity assumptions, but does not adequately address posterior non-identifiability or uncertainty extrapolation. No material ethical violation is apparent; the decisive concern is that the central theoretical reliability claims exceed the evidence, despite promising empirical results.
